questions.prompt: What is a closure in Swift?

options.text: A self-contained block of code that can be passed around and stored in constants or variables.
options.explanation: Right. Closures are first-class code blocks that can be passed as arguments or stored.

options.text: A special struct that can only hold static properties and methods without functions.
options.explanation: Closures are executable blocks of code, not static structs.

options.text: A background thread worker managed exclusively by the operating system kernel.
options.explanation: Closures are language-level blocks of code, not OS threads.

options.text: A memory pointer that always requires manual allocation and deallocation.
options.explanation: Swift manages closure memory automatically.

questions.prompt: What does the in keyword do inside a Swift closure expression?

options.text: It imports external framework packages into the local closure scope.
options.explanation: Frameworks are imported using the import keyword.

options.text: It separates parameter and return type declarations from the closure body statements.
options.explanation: Right. The in keyword marks the start of the execution statements.

options.text: It starts a loop that iterates over each element in a collection.
options.explanation: The for-in loop uses in, but inside a closure expression it separates signature from body.

options.text: It marks the closure as an asynchronous background task.
options.explanation: Asynchronous functions use the async keyword.

questions.prompt: Are closures and functions in Swift value types or reference types?

options.text: They are value types that create duplicate independent copies upon assignment.
options.explanation: Closures are not value types.

options.text: They are value types when defined globally, but reference types when declared inside classes.
options.explanation: All closures and functions are reference types regardless of where they are declared.

options.text: They are reference types, meaning multiple assignments point to the same underlying closure.
options.explanation: Right. Closures are reference types and share captured values.

options.text: They are primitive scalar types that store data directly on the stack.
options.explanation: Closures are reference types, not scalar primitives.

questions.prompt: Which statement accurately describes the relationship between functions and closures in Swift?

options.text: Functions and closures are completely separate types that cannot share signatures.
options.explanation: Functions and closures share the exact same function types.

options.text: Closures are value types, whereas functions are reference types.
options.explanation: Both functions and closures are reference types.

options.text: Closures cannot accept parameters or return values, while functions can.
options.explanation: Closures can accept parameters and return values just like functions.

options.text: Functions are actually special cases of closures that happen to have names.
options.explanation: Right. Global and nested functions are named closures.

questions.prompt: What is trailing closure syntax in Swift?

options.text: Writing a closure expression outside function call parentheses when it is the final argument.
options.explanation: Right. Trailing closure syntax places the closure block after the parentheses.

options.text: Adding a closure parameter at the beginning of a function parameter list.
options.explanation: Trailing closures appear at the end of the argument list, not the beginning.

options.text: Executing a closure after a delayed timer expires on the main thread.
options.explanation: Trailing closure is a syntax feature, not a timer mechanism.

options.text: Appending a semicolon to terminate a closure body statement.
options.explanation: Swift does not use semicolons for trailing closures.

questions.prompt: When can you omit empty parentheses () completely when calling a function with a trailing closure?

options.text: Only when the closure returns void.
options.explanation: The return type does not dictate whether parentheses can be omitted.

options.text: When the closure is the only argument required by the function.
options.explanation: Right. If the closure is the sole argument, empty parentheses are not required.

options.text: Whenever the enclosing function is marked with private access.
options.explanation: Access levels do not affect trailing closure syntax.

options.text: Never, because call parentheses are always strictly mandatory.
options.explanation: Swift explicitly permits omitting parentheses when the closure is the only argument.

questions.prompt: What happens if you try to use $0 inside a closure that already defines explicit parameter names?

options.text: The closure automatically treats $0 as a pointer to the return value.
options.explanation: Shorthand names refer to arguments, not return values.

options.text: The code runs normally because Swift aliases parameter names to numbered positions.
options.explanation: Swift does not allow mixing named parameters with shorthand positional names.

options.text: The compiler produces an error because you cannot mix shorthand and named parameters.
options.explanation: Right. You must choose either explicit parameter names or shorthand arguments.

options.text: The first argument receives a default value of zero.
options.explanation: Shorthand names do not supply default values.

questions.prompt: What do the shorthand argument names $0 and $1 represent inside a closure body?

options.text: Global memory registers used by the Swift runtime engine.
options.explanation: They represent closure arguments, not hardware registers.

options.text: Static counter variables that increment automatically on each call.
options.explanation: They do not increment values automatically.

options.text: Temporary error codes returned from failed operations.
options.explanation: Swift uses Error protocols for errors, not dollar signs.

options.text: The closure parameters referenced by their sequential position.
options.explanation: Right. $0 refers to the first argument, $1 refers to the second, and so on.

questions.prompt: When using shorthand argument names like $0 and $1, what else can be omitted from the closure expression?

options.text: The entire parameter list and the in keyword.
options.explanation: Right. With shorthand names, the parameter declarations and in keyword are omitted.

options.text: The surrounding curly braces around the body.
options.explanation: Curly braces are always required to delimit a closure.

options.text: The statements that evaluate the return value.
options.explanation: The closure still needs executable expressions to compute results.

options.text: The variable that stores the closure instance.
options.explanation: Storing or passing the closure is independent of its internal syntax.

questions.prompt: What does it mean when a closure captures a value from its surrounding context?

options.text: It locks the surrounding variable so that no other function can read it.
options.explanation: Capturing does not lock variables against reading.

options.text: It keeps a reference to the variable so it remains usable even after its enclosing scope ends.
options.explanation: Right. The captured variable stays alive in memory for the closure to use.

options.text: It forces the variable to convert into a global singleton instance in memory.
options.explanation: Captured variables are retained by the closure, not made global singletons.

options.text: It writes the variable directly to persistent storage on the physical device.
options.explanation: Capturing is an in-memory mechanism, not disk storage.

questions.prompt: When can a single-expression closure omit the return keyword?

options.text: Only when the closure returns an optional value.
options.explanation: Optional return types do not determine whether return can be omitted.

options.text: Only when the closure takes zero parameters.
options.explanation: Closures with any number of parameters can omit return if they have a single expression.

options.text: Whenever the closure body consists of a single expression evaluating to the return type.
options.explanation: Right. Swift implicitly returns the value of a single expression.

options.text: Whenever the closure is passed to a background execution queue.
options.explanation: The queue context does not affect implicit return rules.

questions.prompt: Which type of closure has a name and can capture values from its surrounding function?

options.text: A global function.
options.explanation: Global functions have names but do not capture values.

options.text: An inline closure expression.
options.explanation: Closure expressions are unnamed blocks.

options.text: An anonymous closure block.
options.explanation: Anonymous closures do not have names.

options.text: A nested function.
options.explanation: Right. Nested functions are named closures that capture values from enclosing functions.

questions.prompt: Two constants, firstClosure and secondClosure, are assigned the same closure that increments a captured variable. What happens when secondClosure is called?

options.text: It increments the same captured variable shared with firstClosure.
options.explanation: Right. Closures are reference types, so both constants share the same captured state.

options.text: It creates a separate copy with its own independent counter starting at zero.
options.explanation: Closures do not make separate value copies upon assignment.

options.text: It crashes at runtime due to a simultaneous memory access conflict.
options.explanation: Sequential calls to shared closure instances do not crash.

options.text: It resets the captured counter back to its initial value.
options.explanation: Calling a closure does not reset its captured variables.

questions.prompt: Why does Swift allow type inference for parameters and return values inside closure arguments like names.sorted(by:)?

options.text: Because closures are dynamically typed at runtime in Swift.
options.explanation: Swift is statically typed; types are inferred at compile time.

options.text: Because the parameter types and return type are already declared in the method signature.
options.explanation: Right. The sorted(by:) method explicitly expects (Element, Element) -> Bool.

options.text: Because sorted(by:) converts all elements to generic Any types before execution.
options.explanation: Array elements preserve their strong concrete types.

options.text: Because the Swift compiler ignores all type rules inside curly braces.
options.explanation: The compiler checks types strictly inside closures.

questions.prompt: Which of the following closure expressions demonstrates the most idiomatic Swift syntax for sorting an array of numbers in descending order?

options.text: numbers.sorted(by: { (a: Int, b: Int) -> Bool in return a > b })
options.explanation: This syntax is valid but overly verbose in idiomatic Swift.

options.text: numbers.sorted(by: { a, b in return a > b })
options.explanation: This omits types but still includes explicit names and an unnecessary return keyword.

options.text: numbers.sorted { $0 > $1 }
options.explanation: Right. Trailing closure syntax combined with shorthand arguments is idiomatic.

options.text: numbers.sorted() { (a, b) in a > b }
options.explanation: The empty parentheses and explicit parameter names are unnecessary.

questions.prompt: What is a closure in Swift, and how does it relate to a function? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Defines a closure as a self-contained block of functionality that can be passed around and executed
Explains that named functions are special cases of closures
Mentions that closure expressions can be written inline without a formal function name

questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, a closure is a self-contained block of functionality that can be passed and stored. Functions are actually special named closures. Global functions have names without capturing values, while nested functions have names and capture values. Closure expressions are lightweight blocks of code written inline without a name.

questions.prompt: What purpose does the in keyword serve in a Swift closure expression? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that in marks the boundary between the signature and the body
States that the parameter list and return type appear before in
Notes that the execution statements appear after in

questions.modelAnswer: The in keyword marks the separation between a closure declaration and its body statements. Parameters and the return type definition are placed before the in keyword. The executable code statements follow immediately after the in keyword. When shorthand argument names like $0 are used, the in keyword is omitted completely.

questions.prompt: Explain value capturing in Swift closures. What happens to a captured local variable when its enclosing function finishes execution? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that closures capture and store references to constants and variables from surrounding scope
States that captured variables remain alive in memory even after the enclosing function returns
Mentions that the closure retains access to read or mutate the captured variable

questions.modelAnswer: Value capturing allows a closure to reference variables from the surrounding scope where it was defined. Even after the enclosing function finishes execution and leaves the call stack, the captured variable remains alive in memory. The closure retains a reference to the variable, allowing it to read or modify the value across future calls.

questions.prompt: Why are closures reference types in Swift? What happens when you assign a closure instance to multiple constants or variables? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that closures and functions are reference types
States that assigning a closure to multiple variables points them to the same underlying instance
Explains that any captured state is shared across all references

questions.modelAnswer: Closures and functions in Swift are reference types rather than value types. When you assign a closure to multiple constants or variables, each reference points to the exact same closure instance. Any captured state or variables are shared between all references, meaning mutations through one reference reflect in all others.

questions.prompt: Explain trailing closure syntax in Swift. When can the function call parentheses be completely omitted? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that trailing closures can be written outside parentheses when a closure is the final parameter
States that parentheses can be omitted entirely if the closure is the only argument
Notes that this provides clean, readable syntax for higher-order functions

questions.modelAnswer: Trailing closure syntax allows developers to write a closure expression outside function call parentheses when it is the final argument. If the closure is the only argument passed to the function, the empty parentheses can be omitted entirely. This feature produces clean, readable code when working with functions like map, filter, or custom completion handlers.
